examples.title: Diagnosing Why Priya Nair Can't Edit a Field on Her Own Key Account's Opportunity
examples.context: Lesson 11 implements Cascade's security model for real. This worked example is the realistic moment that implementation gets tested: a specific person, on a specific record they clearly should have access to, reports a specific, narrow problem — exactly the kind of ticket a real Salesforce Administrator gets constantly.
examples.objective: Given a user who can view an Opportunity record but can't edit one specific field on it, use the layered security troubleshooting order to find the real cause — not the first plausible-sounding guess — and fix it with the minimum correct change.
examples.startingInformation:
**The ticket:** Priya Nair reports she can open the Opportunity for Riverside Hospitality Group — one of her own Key Accounts — and can see every field on it, including the deal value. But when she tries to update the **Close Date** field ahead of a renegotiation, the field is greyed out. She can edit every other field on the same record without issue.

**What's already confirmed:** Priya owns this Opportunity. She is a Sales Rep profile. The record is clearly visible to her (she can open it and see all its data).
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — Apply the layered order, starting from what the symptom actually tells you.** The record is visible and most fields are editable — that already rules out layers 1 (object permissions), 3 (OWD), 4 (role hierarchy), and 5 (sharing rules) as the cause, since all four of those control whether she can reach the *record* at all, and she clearly can. A problem scoped to exactly one field, on a record she otherwise has full access to, points directly at layer 2: field-level security.

**Step 2 — Resist the instinct to start with OWD or sharing rules anyway.** This is the single most common mistake in diagnosing this exact symptom: OWD and sharing rules are the first things people think of when a security ticket comes in, because they're the most commonly discussed. But neither one operates at the single-field grain — they're both record-level controls. Starting there on a single-field symptom wastes investigation time on layers the symptom has already ruled out.

**Step 3 — Check the Sales Rep profile's field-level security on Close Date specifically.** Object Manager → Opportunity → Fields & Relationships → Close Date → Field-Level Security — the Sales Rep profile shows Read checked, Edit unchecked.

**Step 4 — Confirm this is deliberate, not a mistake, before "fixing" it.** Check Lesson 4's security design and the automation inventory: is there a business reason Close Date is locked for Sales Reps specifically? In this case, there isn't one documented — it reads as an oversight from when the Sales Rep profile was cloned from a template that happened to lock that field, not an intentional Cascade business rule.
examples.reasoning: The reasoning worth internalizing is in Step 1-2: a symptom's *shape* — record-level versus field-level — tells you which layers are even in play before you check anything. Priya being able to see and edit every other field on a record she clearly has full record-level access to is strong evidence the problem lives at exactly one layer, and starting the investigation somewhere else (because OWD and sharing rules are more commonly discussed in training material) wastes time disproving layers the symptom already ruled out. This is also why the troubleshooting checklist's layered order matters as an *order*, not just a list — working top to bottom, and reading what each layer actually controls, gets you to field-level security in two steps instead of five.
examples.solution:
```text
Object Manager -> Opportunity -> Fields & Relationships -> Close Date
-> Field-Level Security -> Sales Rep profile

Before: Visible (checked), Read-Only (checked) -- i.e. Read allowed,
         Edit not allowed
After:  Visible (checked), Read-Only (unchecked) -- Edit now allowed
```

```text
Since no documented business reason locks this field for Sales Reps,
and the Sales Manager profile correctly has Edit access (confirmed
by checking Derek Oyelaran's profile for comparison), the fix is
enabling Edit on Close Date for the Sales Rep profile specifically --
not creating a new permission set, which would be solving a
single-profile oversight with more infrastructure than the problem
needs.
```
examples.validation: Confirm Priya can now edit Close Date on the test record. Confirm no other field's FLS was touched. Confirm a different Sales Rep (e.g. Tom Baptiste) also gained Edit access on Close Date, since the fix was made at the profile level and should apply to every Sales Rep, not just Priya specifically.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Starting the investigation at OWD or sharing rules** because they're the most familiar security concepts, instead of reading what the symptom's shape (record-level vs. field-level) already rules out.
- **Creating a new permission set to grant Priya Edit access individually**, instead of fixing the profile-level setting that's actually wrong for every Sales Rep — this would mask the real scope of the problem and leave every other Sales Rep with the same bug.
- **Widening Edit access without checking whether the restriction was deliberate first** — in this case it wasn't, but assuming that without checking Lesson 4's design is how an intentional business rule gets accidentally undone.

examples.title: Scaling Cascade's Sample Data Without Breaking the Lead Auto-Assignment Flow
examples.context: Lesson 16 loads a realistic but modest volume of sample data. This worked example asks a realistic follow-up: what happens to Lesson 12's New Lead Auto-Assignment Flow when 500 Leads land at once instead of one at a time — the kind of volume a real trade-show follow-up or a purchased list import would actually produce.
examples.objective: Load 500 test Leads in one batch, confirm the New Lead Auto-Assignment Flow (sets Owner to Jordan Kessler, creates a follow-up Task) handles the volume correctly, and fix it if it doesn't — applying Category 6's bulk-safety requirement for real.
examples.startingInformation: **The Flow being tested, from Lesson 12's documentation:** a record-triggered, after-save Flow on Lead that sets Owner to Jordan Kessler and creates a follow-up Task due tomorrow, for every new Lead. **The test:** import 500 Leads via Data Loader in a single batch, rather than creating them one at a time through the UI the way the Flow was originally built and clicked-through during development.
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — Run the bulk load and watch for governor-limit failures, not just whether Leads were created.** All 500 Leads insert successfully — but checking Setup → Flow → the Flow's run history shows a subset of records (specifically, Leads in the later sub-batches of the 500-record load) have no follow-up Task created, with no visible error on the Lead records themselves.

**Step 2 — Check what Lesson 12's Flow actually does inside its own logic, not just what it's documented to do.** Opening the Flow shows the Task-creation step uses a single Create Records element configured to run once *per Lead*, inside what's effectively a per-record context rather than using a bulkified "collect then create once" pattern.

**Step 3 — Identify the actual limit being hit.** Record-triggered Flows process in batches of 200 records per transaction. Each Lead in the batch individually stays within DML limits — but the Flow's Task-creation step, as built, issues one DML operation per Lead rather than collecting all needed Task records into a single bulk DML call, which is exactly the inefficient, non-bulk-safe pattern Flow Bulkification material warns against. Depending on what else is running in the same transaction, this either silently degrades or fails partway through the batch once enough per-record DML operations stack up.

**Step 4 — Confirm this exact failure never surfaced during original development**, because every test during Lesson 12 and Lesson 17 created Leads one at a time through the UI, where each Lead triggers its own separate transaction with the Flow comfortably inside every limit.
examples.reasoning: This is the real lesson Category 6's bulk-safety requirement is pointing at: a Flow that works perfectly in every manual, one-record-at-a-time test can still fail specifically under bulk conditions that single-record testing structurally can never exercise. The failure isn't a logic bug — the Flow's business logic (assign to Jordan, create a follow-up Task) is completely correct — it's a *volume* bug, which is exactly why Category 6 requires a bulk test specifically, separate from and in addition to the single-record test plan in Lesson 17. A test plan with only single-record checks would have passed 100% and still shipped this defect.
examples.solution:
```text
Fix: restructure the Flow's Task-creation logic to collect Task
records for the whole triggering batch into a collection variable,
then create them with a single bulk "Create Records" action outside
any per-record loop -- the same before/after bulkification pattern
covered in the Flow Automation course's performance lesson, applied
here for real instead of as a worked example.
```

```text
Re-test: reload the same 500-Lead batch after the fix. Confirm via
the Flow's run history that every one of the 500 Leads has a
corresponding follow-up Task, not just the ones in the first
sub-batch.
```
examples.validation: Re-run the 500-Lead bulk import after the fix and confirm all 500 resulting Leads have both Owner correctly set to Jordan Kessler and a follow-up Task created — check the full 500, not a sample, since the original failure was specifically in later sub-batches. Confirm single-record Lead creation through the UI still works correctly too, since a bulkification fix shouldn't change the Flow's behavior for the original, already-passing test case.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Only testing with Leads created one at a time**, which is exactly how this defect stayed hidden through the original build and test-plan lessons — bulk testing has to be a deliberate, separate test, not an extension of single-record testing.
- **Assuming "some Leads worked fine" means the Flow is basically okay** — a defect that only affects records in later sub-batches of a large load is still a real production risk, just one that's easy to miss if only the first few results are checked.
- **Treating this as a logic bug and rewriting the assignment/Task-creation business rule** — the actual business logic was correct the whole time; the fix is purely about how the DML operations are batched, not what they do.

examples.title: Planning Cascade's Move From a Developer Edition Org to Real Production
examples.context: Lesson 18 is honest that this capstone was built entirely in one org and never practices moving between environments. This worked example closes that gap specifically for Category 7 of the acceptance rubric — not by actually performing a deployment (this capstone doesn't have a second org to deploy to), but by producing the real, specific plan a working administrator would need before doing one.
examples.objective: Write a real, specific change-management and rollback plan for moving Cascade's finished build from the Developer Edition org it was built in to a production org, naming an actual sequence and a genuine rollback target for the highest-risk component.
examples.startingInformation: **What exists:** a complete build in one Developer Edition org — the security model, custom objects, Flows, validation rules, an approval process, reports/dashboards, and sample data. **What doesn't exist:** a second (production) org, any prior deployment history, or any change set already created. **The constraint:** change sets can only move metadata (objects, fields, Flows, security settings) — they cannot move data, so the realistic sample data from Lesson 16 is explicitly out of scope for this deployment plan.
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — Sequence the deployment by dependency, not by build order.** The build order in this capstone (data model → security → automation → reports) happened to also be close to a safe deployment order, but that's worth verifying rather than assuming: custom objects and fields must deploy before any Flow or validation rule that references them, and the security model (profiles, OWD, sharing rules) should deploy with or immediately after the objects they govern, before any end user could access an object with the wrong default visibility even briefly.

**Step 2 — Decide what gets validated before anything goes live for real users.** A deployment to production should run through Salesforce's "Validate Only" deployment option first (or an equivalent check-only deploy), which runs all the same tests and checks as a real deployment without actually making the change — catching a metadata dependency problem before it affects a real user, not after.

**Step 3 — Name the single highest-risk component and plan its rollback specifically, per the rubric's requirement.** Of everything in this build, the security model carries the most risk if something goes wrong — a misconfigured OWD or sharing rule deployed to production could briefly expose sensitive Key Accounts data org-wide, not just cause an error. The rollback plan for this component specifically: deploy security changes in their own, isolated change set (not bundled with objects/Flows), so a problem can be reverted by deploying a correction to just that change set, without having to also pull back unrelated custom-object or Flow changes.

**Step 4 — Be explicit about what this plan doesn't cover, matching Lesson 18's own honesty standard.** This capstone never actually tested a real deployment, never validated this plan against a real second org, and the sample data strategy for a real production rollout (which would need real customer data, not Lesson 16's realistic-but-fictional sample data) is a genuinely different problem not addressed here at all.
examples.reasoning: The judgment call worth defending in an interview is Step 3's decision to isolate the security model into its own change set, separate from objects and automation. The temptation with a small build like this one is to bundle everything into a single deployment for simplicity — but the actual risk profile of a security misconfiguration (potential data exposure, not just a broken feature) is different in kind from the risk of a broken Flow (an inconvenience, fixable without exposure risk), and a rollback plan should scope its blast radius to match that difference. Treating every component as equally risky, bundled into one all-or-nothing deployment, is the easy default that a real change-management plan specifically has to push back against.
examples.solution:
```markdown
# Cascade CMS — Deployment & Rollback Plan

## Deployment sequence
1. Custom objects and fields (Installation Project, Service Contract,
   and all custom fields) -- Change Set 1
2. Security model (profiles, OWD, sharing rules) -- Change Set 2,
   deployed separately from Change Set 1 and 3 specifically for
   rollback isolation
3. Automation (Flows, validation rules, approval process) -- Change
   Set 3, deployed only after 1 and 2 are confirmed live
4. Reports and dashboards -- Change Set 4

## Validation step
Every change set runs through Validate Only first. No change set
proceeds to a real deployment until its validation step reports zero
errors.

## Rollback plan: security model (highest risk)
If a security misconfiguration is discovered post-deployment:
1. Immediately revert OWD on the affected object(s) to the most
   restrictive setting (Private) as an emergency stopgap -- this can
   be done directly in Setup, faster than redeploying a change set.
2. Deploy a corrected version of Change Set 2 specifically, isolated
   from Change Sets 1/3/4, which were never implicated.
3. Re-validate affected users' actual access via Login As before
   declaring the rollback complete.

## Known limitations of this plan
This plan has not been tested against a real second org -- this
capstone was built entirely in one Developer Edition org. Data
migration strategy for real production (vs. Lesson 16's fictional
sample data) is out of scope here and would need its own plan.
```
examples.validation: Confirm the plan names a real, specific sequence (not "deploy everything") and a real, specific rollback target (not "roll back if something breaks"). Confirm the plan's honesty section matches Lesson 18's own standard — explicit about what wasn't actually tested, not implying more confidence than the capstone's own single-org build supports.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Bundling the security model into the same change set as everything else** for simplicity, losing the ability to roll it back in isolation if it's the one component that goes wrong.
- **Skipping the Validate Only step** to save time, trading a safe pre-check for the risk of a partially-failed real deployment.
- **Writing a rollback plan that says "redeploy the previous version"** without naming which specific change set, which is not actually specific enough to execute under real pressure.
